The first computer 'bug' was a real moth.
In 1947, engineers found a moth stuck in a relay of the Harvard Mark II computer and taped it into their logbook as the 'first actual case of bug being found'.
The first webcam was pointed at a coffee pot.
In 1991, scientists at Cambridge University set it up so they could check from their desks whether the pot was empty.
The first video on YouTube is 19 seconds long and filmed at a zoo.
'Me at the zoo' was uploaded in April 2005 by co-founder Jawed Karim, standing in front of elephants.
The @ sign in email addresses was picked in 1971.
Ray Tomlinson sent the first email between two computers and chose @ because it was not used in anyone's name.
The first text message said 'Merry Christmas'.
Engineer Neil Papworth sent it from a computer to a phone in December 1992. Phones could not type messages yet.
Wi-Fi does not stand for anything.
It is a brand name invented by a marketing company in 1999. 'Wireless fidelity' was added later and is not official.
Bluetooth is named after a Viking king.
Harald 'Bluetooth' united Danish tribes in the 900s. The logo joins his initials written in old Nordic runes.
The Python programming language is named after a comedy show, not a snake.
Its creator, Guido van Rossum, was a fan of 'Monty Python's Flying Circus'.
Linux was started in 1991 as 'just a hobby'.
Finnish student Linus Torvalds said it would not be 'big and professional'. Today it runs most web servers and every Android phone.
Git, the tool programmers use to track code, was written in about ten days.
Linus Torvalds made it in 2005 after Linux lost its free access to another tool.
The first .com website name ever registered was symbolics.com.
A computer company registered it on 15 March 1985. The address still exists.
Google is named after a misspelled huge number.
A googol is 1 followed by 100 zeros. The founders wanted a name that suggested endless information.
Amazon was nearly called Cadabra.
Jeff Bezos dropped the name partly because, over the phone, it sounded like 'cadaver', a dead body.
The first iPhone had no app store.
It came out in 2007 with only Apple's own apps. The App Store opened a year later, in 2008, with about 500 apps.
Nokia began as a paper mill in 1865.
Over time it made rubber boots, tyres and cables before turning to mobile phones.
Samsung started by selling dried fish and noodles.
It began in 1938 as a small trading company in Korea, long before it made electronics.
Nintendo is more than 130 years old.
It was founded in 1889 in Kyoto to make hand-painted playing cards called hanafuda.
Tetris was made in the Soviet Union in 1984.
Alexey Pajitnov built it on a computer with no graphics, so the first blocks were drawn with brackets and spaces.
The first emoji set had 176 tiny pictures.
Shigetaka Kurita designed them for a Japanese phone company in 1999. The original set is now kept at the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
Many computers will have a clock problem in January 2038.
Systems that count seconds since 1970 in a 32-bit number will run out of space at 03:14:07 on 19 January 2038 (world time).
Almost all the internet traffic between countries travels through cables on the sea floor.
There are hundreds of these cables. Bangladesh connects through cables landing at Cox's Bazar and Kuakata.
The first computer mouse was made of wood.
Douglas Engelbart built it in the 1960s with two metal wheels underneath. It was called a mouse because the wire looked like a tail.
In 1968 one demo showed the mouse, video calls and links between documents.
Douglas Engelbart's show is called 'the Mother of All Demos' because so much of today's computing appeared in it first.
ENIAC, one of the first computers, weighed about 27 tonnes.
Built in 1945, it used around 18,000 glass vacuum tubes and filled a large room.
The first computer program was written about 100 years before computers existed.
In 1843, Ada Lovelace wrote steps for Charles Babbage's planned Analytical Engine to calculate a series of numbers.
Junk email is called spam because of a comedy sketch.
In a Monty Python sketch, a café serves the tinned meat Spam with everything while people sing 'spam' over and over.
The first online banner ad was clicked by 44 percent of people who saw it.
It appeared in 1994 and asked 'Have you ever clicked your mouse right HERE?'. Today most ads get clicked far less than 1 percent of the time.
QR codes were invented to track car parts.
Denso Wave, part of the Toyota group, created them in 1994. A QR code can still be read even when part of it is damaged.
The first product scanned with a barcode was a pack of chewing gum.
It happened at a shop in Ohio, USA, in June 1974.
The inventor of the lithium-ion battery won a Nobel Prize at 97.
John Goodenough shared the 2019 chemistry prize, making him the oldest Nobel winner ever. These batteries power phones and laptops.
White LED lights only became possible after blue LEDs were invented.
Red and green LEDs existed for decades. Three scientists cracked blue in the early 1990s and won the 2014 Nobel Prize in physics.
The word 'robot' comes from a 1920 play.
Czech writer Karel Čapek used it in 'R.U.R.'. It comes from 'robota', meaning forced work.
Alan Turing suggested a test for thinking machines in 1950.
He called it 'the imitation game': if a person cannot tell whether they are chatting with a human or a machine, the machine passes.
The words 'artificial intelligence' were first used in 1955.
John McCarthy and others used them in a plan for a summer workshop at Dartmouth College in 1956.
An AI's single surprising move in 2016 stunned the world of Go.
AlphaGo's 'move 37' against champion Lee Sedol looked like a mistake to experts, then turned out to be brilliant. AlphaGo won the match 4 to 1.
Your 1 TB hard drive shows up as about 931 GB for a reason.
Makers count 1 GB as 1,000,000,000 bytes, but computers count in powers of 2, so the same space looks smaller.
The first phone with a built-in camera was sold in Japan in 2000.
The Sharp J-SH04 took pictures of about 0.1 megapixels, tiny compared with phone cameras today.
The hashtag on social media was suggested by a user, not the company.
Chris Messina proposed using # to group posts on Twitter in 2007. Twitter added clickable hashtags in 2009.
Website 'cookies' got their name from programmers' slang.
Lou Montulli at Netscape used the term in 1994, borrowing 'magic cookie', a small bit of data passed between programs.
CAPTCHA puzzles once helped turn old books into text.
The reCAPTCHA project had people type words that scanning software could not read, digitising millions of words from books and newspapers.
The Apollo spacecraft computer that went to the Moon had about 4 KB of working memory.
Its programs were woven by hand into 'rope memory', with wires threaded through or around tiny magnetic rings.
In 1956 a 5 MB hard drive weighed about a tonne.
IBM's RAMAC had fifty spinning metal discs, each about 60 cm wide, and had to be moved by forklift.
GPS is free for everyone, but it is run by a space force.
The US Space Force operates it. Europe's Galileo, Russia's GLONASS and China's BeiDou are other systems your phone may also use.
The Java programming language was first called Oak.
It was named after a tree outside the creator's office, but the name was already taken, so it became Java, after coffee.
Ctrl+Alt+Delete was meant as a secret shortcut for programmers.
IBM engineer David Bradley chose keys far apart so no one would press them by accident.
The first tweet was posted in March 2006.
Jack Dorsey wrote 'just setting up my twttr'. The service had dropped its vowels at first.
The Internet Archive has saved hundreds of billions of old web pages.
Its Wayback Machine lets you see how websites looked years ago, even ones that have since disappeared.
The first website is still online.
Tim Berners-Lee published it at CERN in 1991 to explain the World Wide Web. CERN restored it at its original address.
The very first computer game for fun may be from 1958.
'Tennis for Two' ran on an oscilloscope screen at a US lab, made by physicist William Higinbotham to entertain visitors.
The ARPANET, the internet's ancestor, crashed on its first message.
In 1969 a student tried to type 'LOGIN' between two computers. The system crashed after 'LO'.
Most Bangla typing on computers uses Unicode, which gives each letter a number.
Bangla letters live in a block of code numbers from U+0980 to U+09FF, so they look the same on every device.
Morse code was used for ship distress calls for almost 100 years.
SOS was chosen because its dots and dashes are easy to send and recognise. Morse distress calls officially ended in 1999.
Early mobile phones were called 'bricks'.
The first handheld mobile call was made in 1973 on a Motorola phone weighing about 1 kg, with 30 minutes of talk time.
Some data centres are cooled with seawater or placed in cold countries.
Computers make lots of heat, so companies build data centres near the Arctic Circle or use lake and sea water for cooling.
Computer chips are made in rooms thousands of times cleaner than a hospital.
A single speck of dust can ruin a chip, so workers wear full 'bunny suits' and air is filtered constantly.
A modern phone chip holds well over 10 billion tiny switches.
These transistors are so small that more than a thousand could sit side by side across the width of a human hair.
